answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Microsoft.DocumentDB/resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (i.e. provider namespace Microsoft.DocumentDB and resource type databaseAccounts).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). Example: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --locations regionName=westus2 --kind MongoDB

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: resource of type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts' (apiVersion e.g. '2021-04-15') with properties set for MongoDB API. Terraform (azurerm provider): resource 'azurerm_cosmosdb_account' (optionally with azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database/collection for MongoDB-specific children).

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: MongoDB-style URI. Example pattern for a Cosmos DB Mongo endpoint: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>&maxIdleTimeMS=120000 . Host suffix is '<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com' and port is 10255; options must include ssl=true (TLS), replicaSet=globaldb and usually retryWrites=false for Cosmos Mongo API.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is billed as Request Units (RU/s) for Cosmos DB accounts (including MongoDB API), with options for provisioned throughput (fixed RU/s), autoscale, and in some accounts serverless mode. It is not billed directly by vCore for standard Cosmos DB accounts.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB-compatible API you typically use the account username/password (the primary/secondary keys exposed by the account) and SCRAM-style auth (SCRAM-SHA). Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) token-based authentication is not generally available for the Cosmos Mongo API (Azure AD integration exists for other Cosmos APIs), so the driver normally authenticates with the credentials in the MongoDB URI. (If Azure AD support is required, you would use the supported Cosmos DB API that exposes Azure AD auth.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: For MongoDB-compatible workloads use the standard MongoDB drivers (e.g. pymongo for Python, MongoDB Node.js driver). There is no separate 'DocumentDB' mongo client; for non-Mongo APIs you would use the azure-cosmos SDK. So use pymongo.MongoClient(connection_string) in Python.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: My expectation: the Cosmos DB Mongo-compatible API historically did not provide built-in vector index primitives. If vector indexes are available on a managed Mongo interface they'd follow MongoDB/Atlas style createIndex syntax for knn/ANN (e.g. a knn_vector or search index). An example I would try (if supported) is: db.products.createIndex({embedding: 'knn_vector'}, {knn: {algorithm:'hnsw', dimensions:1536, M:16, efConstruction:200}}). Note: this is speculative — if the service exposes vector index types they will follow Mongo/Atlas or proprietary options; otherwise you must store vectors and use an external vector search engine or Azure Cognitive Search + custom scoring.

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Use Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) integrated with Cosmos DB for full-text and hybrid search. Cosmos DB does not provide a built-in advanced full-text engine with ranking like Azure Cognitive Search, so the common pattern is to index Cosmos data into an Azure Cognitive Search index using indexers or push indexing.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: My recollection: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API historically supported selected MongoDB server versions/wire protocols (older accounts supported 3.2/3.6, newer accounts up to 4.x/5.x depending on the account's API version). Many advanced MongoDB server features may be missing or behave differently (server-side JS, some aggregation stages, certain index types, some transaction semantics), so expect some incompatibilities. Exact supported server protocol version must be checked per-account in the portal/CLI.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is an Azure Cosmos DB Emulator but historically it supports Core (SQL), Gremlin, Table and Cassandra, not the MongoDB API. For MongoDB-compatible development use a local MongoDB Docker image: docker run -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo -d mongo:latest and connect on mongodb://localhost:27017. For testing against the real service use the provided cluster endpoint (DOCUMENTDB_URI).

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: For Cosmos DB the canonical change notification mechanism is the Change Feed (SQL API). The MongoDB-style change streams are not universally supported across the MongoDB API on Cosmos; many Cosmos Mongo API accounts do not support MongoDB change streams. To get change notifications you normally use Cosmos DB's Change Feed on the container (enabled by default for supported APIs) or the service-specific streaming features.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Based on the sample environment, the 'documentdb' MCP server is the one that provides data-plane tools tailored to this service; the general Azure MCP server does not expose the same documentdb-specific inspection tools. (Use the 'documentdb' MCP server profile named 'default' to inspect collections/indexes/query plans.)

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name of Microsoft's JSON document database service; it was rebranded/evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. The old 'DocumentDB' name refers to the original Cosmos SQL API; the Cosmos MongoDB API is a separate compatibility layer that implements the MongoDB wire protocol. This service is Microsoft-managed and distinct from any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath is Microsoft's proprietary Cosmos DB engine with a MongoDB-protocol compatibility layer for the Mongo API. That means you use MongoDB drivers in your app, but some server behaviors, features, and semantics may differ from a native MongoDB server — expect some feature gaps and differences in indexing/transactions/aggregation — so test for compatibility.

answers.question: Which database name should the sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named 'sample_retail_13' for all sample-created objects and queries.

answers.question: Which Python client will the sample use to connect to DocumentDB and how should it obtain the connection URI?
answers.answer: Use pymongo: from pymongo import MongoClient; conn = MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'], tls=True). Read the full MongoDB URI from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime (do not store credentials in files).

answers.question: What collection and vector index definition will the sample attempt to create for product vectors?
answers.answer: Create a 'products' collection in database 'sample_retail_13' and create a vector ANN index on the embedding field. Example (Mongo-style syntax I will try): db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'knn_vector' }, { name: 'embedding_vec', knn: { algorithm: 'hnsw', dimensions: 1536, M: 16, efConstruction: 200 } }) — if the managed cluster supports knn_vector/HNSW. If that exact syntax fails, fall back to storing vectors and using an external vector search or the cluster's recommended vector-index command.

answers.question: How should the sample authenticate when connecting and what TLS options are required?
answers.answer: Use the credentials embedded in DOCUMENTDB_URI (username/password). Ensure TLS is enabled in the driver (tls=True / ssl=true in the URI). Do not disable certificate validation in production; for sample/tests rely on the server certificate (set tlsAllowInvalidCertificates only if explicitly needed for dev).

answers.question: Which collections does the sample create and what minimal schema/keys will they have?
answers.answer: Create a 'products' collection in 'sample_retail_13'. Each document will contain at least: { productId: <string>, title: <string>, description: <string>, specs: <object>, reviews: [<objects>], embedding: <array<float>> }. Use productId as the application-level unique key (and _id for Mongo if desired).
